transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump is heading back to Washington, D.C., after a four-day trip in Asia.
NPR's Franco Ordoni reports Trump plans to hold a press conference about the trip tomorrow
at the White House.
>> U.S. presidents typically hold a news conference at the end of foreign trips in order to highlight
all that happened behind the scenes and explain what was accomplished.
But President Trump left China without meeting with the press.
Now, China has a history of controlling the media, including banning one U.S. reporter
this trip after she shouted a question during the event.
And it wasn't until the flight back and after President Putin held his own press conference
that Trump announced on social media that he would be holding a press conference at
the White House.
>> In addition to discussing the historic trilateral meeting with China and Russia,
Trump says he'll also be discussing trade deals with Thailand and the Philippines.
Franco Ordoni is NPR News.
>> The Senate rejected a measure today aimed at reining in President Trump's Iran war
and Piers Barber Sproun reports.
>> The Senate voted against a House-adopted measure that would direct President Trump
to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran.
It was a largely party-line vote.
Three Republicans, Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Rand
Paul of Kentucky voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution.
All Democrats supported it except Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman.
Had it passed, it would have largely been symbolic.
Administrations from both parties have long sidestepped Congress in terms of war powers.
Barbara Sproun, NPR News, the Capitol.
>> The United Nations top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the
Rohingya Muslim minority during a 2017 military operation.
It's the first time the International Court of Justice has ruled a state-committed genocide.
The ruling could impact other genocide allegations, including those linked to the Gaza conflict
and the war in Ukraine.
The Army has delayed until Monday its plan to detonate about five tons of bomb-making
chemicals at an ammunition plant in southeast Iowa that spurred concerns.
The detonation was scheduled for tomorrow in Middletown, and military officials recommended
residents leave town.
The detonation is expected to send a plume of toxic lead dust into the air.
Dr. Robert McSell, the medical director for Mercy One Genesis Community Care and Occupational
Health in the Quad Cities area, says the air will be safe as long as exposure is brief.
>> Right after the detonation, there will be lead dust in the air, and you can breathe
that in, and then that can enter the bloodstream.
However, that brief exposure is not gonna be enough to cause any long-term harm effects.
>> The acting army secretary says delaying the detonation until Monday would be the latest
moment before a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of
the material.
The stock market tumbled again today.
This is NPR News.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnhams is meeting with EU officials tomorrow to discuss closer
ties with the block that it left in 2020.
Burnham wants to undo what he says is the damage caused by Brexit, and has suggested
that rejoining the EU is a future possibility.
It's a shift from the previous silence of British governments on reversing Brexit.
Singaporean entrepreneur Jack Sim invented World Toilet Day 25 years ago today, and NPR's
Mark Silver reports.
>> Sim wanted a day to devote attention to the fact that billions of people around the
world cannot find a safe and sanitary toilet.
It was adopted by the UN as an official day in 2013.
This year's theme is sanitation and gender equality.
Girls and women who don't have a toilet at home may venture out in unsafe areas that
makes them vulnerable to attack or harassment.
If their school or office does not offer sanitary facilities, they may opt to stay home during
menstruation.
Despite all the serious issues around toilets, it's okay to be joyful on World Toilet Day,
says Kate Olive-Medlakat with the World Health Organization.
World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year.
It's really important, and it's an opportunity for us to celebrate and act on something that
many of us take for granted.
>> Four in 10 people still do not have access to safe and sanitary toilets.
Mark Silver, NPR News.
>> San Diego County has hired more than 500 goats to help clean up brush and grass to
prevent wildfires.
According to CalMatters, the pilot program is meant to reduce vegetation around homes,
key roads, and in areas that may be needed as evacuation sites and have been aided by
five dogs who helped manage the herd.
This is NPR News.
>> This message comes from NPR sponsor Charles Schwab.
When is the right time to sell a stock?
How do you protect against inflation?
Financial decisions can be tricky, and often, your own cognitive and emotional biases can
lead you astray.
Financial decoder, an original podcast from Charles Schwab, can help.
Again, host Mark Reapie, as he offers practical solutions to help overcome the cognitive and
emotional biases that may affect your investing decisions.
Download the latest episode and subscribe at Schwab.com/financialdecoder.

topics.text: Trump returns from Asia trip; White House press conference planned, after skipping press in China
Senate rejects House-passed measure directing Trump to end U.S. military hostilities with Iran
UN top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims in 2017 military operation
Army delays detonation of five tons of bomb-making chemicals at Iowa ammunition plant until Monday
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to meet EU officials on closer ties, possibly rejoining
World Toilet Day marks 25 years; four in 10 people still lack safe sanitation
San Diego County hires more than 500 goats to clear brush and reduce wildfire risk
